UK Drug Tsar Completes Americanization
By Becoming Utterly Incoherent On Why Marijuana Is Not A "Soft Drug"

(Marijuananews note: When officials are quoted in an article saying something that makes them look foolish, one can always hope that they were misquoted, or taken out of context, etc. But when they go to the trouble to write a letter to the editor of the most prestigious newspaper in the kingdom, alas, one knows for sure.

Here the UK Drug Tsar goes out of his way to make sure that the confusion is his alone.

The point of all this is that in order to have a coherent and successful "drugs" policy, one must first have a coherent and successful marijuana policy, and separate marijuana from the rest.

There are two reasons for this.

First, marijuana is by far the most widely used illicit drug. In the UK it accounts for over 70% of all drug arrests. Second, it is far less dangerous than any of the other drugs, legal or illegal.

Hellawell has set out to prove my point the hard way, by doing just the opposite of what he should. The immediate product is incoherence. The longer term will bring disaster.

It would be so easy for him to look at the Dutch and see what works, and at DEAland and see what does not. In stead, he is ignoring a nearby success and copying a distant failure.)

‘SOFT’ AND ‘HARD’ DRUGS

See
UK Drug Tsar Becoming A Leftwing Bill Bennett;
Combining Puritanism, Irrationality and Class War -- 2 Articles
and links

January 14, 1999
From The London Times
http://www.the-times.co.uk/
letters@the-times.co.uk
By Keith Hellawell, UK Anti-Drugs Co-ordinator

I am not alone in maintaining that any attempt to draw a distinction between so called ‘hard’ and ‘soft’ drugs is unrealistic (letters, January 6) and even dangerous in seeking to wish away the proven harm that drugs like amphetamines and cannabis can do to their users: I have not experienced any disagreement with any minister on this.

(Marijuananews note: "Amphetamines and cannabis?" First, has anyone said that amphetamines are "soft" drugs??? Second, isn’t this rather like saying that I disagree with Hitler and Hellawell? After all, both have advocated arresting people they disapprove of. There may be certain relevant distinctions, however. Third, he says that he has "not experienced any disagreement with any minister on this." Any minister? Was he expecting a member of the government to appear to be "pro-pot" to the Drug Tsar? This is perhaps the antithesis of scientific polling. The margin of error is one hundred percent.)

All drugs

Second, the alternative premise was not that a "soft" drug, basically cannabis, is never harmful in some way. The Dutch use the term "acceptable risk" to describe their view of cannabis.

You know the Dutch? Those rather tall, English speaking people with a much lower rate of all illicit drug use. It is just a short flight.)

Guidance and information

I have acknowledged that some drugs cause particular damage to individuals and the community, and that we should address their availability and misuse as a particular priority.

If all that mattered was the law, then this might be marginally acceptable as a step in the right direction, but substance abuse is a real problem in the UK that clearly cannot be honestly addressed under the present policies. Words matter. Ideas matter.)

This does not mean that we have given up on the others. All our objectives must be to reduce young people’s drug misuse, to reduce drug-related crime, to increase participation in effective treatment programmes and reduce the availability of drugs.
(Marijuananews note: "All our objectives?" Again, no priorities and no distinctions. No consistency. No coherence.)

All these initiatives are embodied in the new ten-year strategy, TACKLING DRUGS TO BUILD A BETTER BRITAIN.

(Marijuananews note: This in the land of Shakespeare and Churchill? Oh yes, it is the land of Orwell, too. Perhaps it is also the land of McCaffrey. The DEAland Drug Czar outlined his own ten-year plan. Hellawell forgot one big difference. Blair may still be in office in ten years. Clinton will be gone in two, max.)

To achieve them Government departments and agencies - both statutory and voluntary - are increasingly working closely together at local, national and international level. Drug action teams across the country have recently submitted to me their action plans for the coming year: and over 200 million pounds extra has been allocated over the next three years for anti-drugs activity.

This will fund programmes to reduce drug-related crime and to get those with the most serious problems into treatment and rehabilitation, as well as supporting the development of more sustained and better prevention and education programmes in schools and community settings. I shall report progress and set out an annual plan of action for the United Kingdom in the spring.
(Marijuananews note: For every action plan, there is an equal and opposite action plan. It is called human behavior in the real world. Bad policies are not just failures; they are counterproductive.)

KEITH HELLAWELL

UK Ant-Drugs Co-ordinator
